question: Weren't the Gospels written decades after Jesus by people who never met him?

ledger.heading: Twelfth run (2026-11-20): the editor's read of the text area's five, and the area "Who wrote the Gospels, when, and the canon"

shortAnswer: On the dating most scholars hold, they were written decades later, and at least two of their authors, on the church's own account, were not among Jesus' followers. Most scholars place Mark around 70, Matthew and Luke between about 75 and 95, and John in the 90s, some forty to sixty-five years after the crucifixion; a minority, with serious arguments, dates some of them earlier. But a gap of that size means something different from what the objection implies. It sits inside a single lifetime, when people who had known Jesus were still alive, and before the Gospels we already have Paul's letters, written in the 50s, which hand on a summary of the core of the story that most scholars think took shape within a few years of the events. Historians of the ancient world work with far larger gaps than this. What the dates can't settle is whether the tradition was kept faithfully in the meantime, and that is the harder question, taken up on the next page.

sections.heading: The objection at its strongest
sections.body:
Jesus was crucified around the year 30. The first Gospel, Mark, was written around 70, on the view most critical scholars hold, and the others came later, John perhaps as late as the 90s. That leaves forty years before anyone wrote his life down, and more than sixty for the last of the four. In those decades the stories passed from mouth to mouth, across languages, from Aramaic-speaking villages in Galilee to Greek-speaking cities around the Mediterranean.

Bart Ehrman puts the point sharply in *Jesus Before the Gospels* (2016). The Gospel writers, he argues, didn't see what they describe and had no contact with anyone who did. They were educated, Greek-speaking Christians, a generation or more removed from the events, writing down what their communities told. And the dates, the objection adds, aren't a hostile guess. They rest on evidence in the texts. Mark has Jesus foretell that not one stone of the temple will be left on another, and the temple was destroyed by the Romans in the year 70. Luke has Jesus speak of Jerusalem surrounded by armies and of enemies building a barricade around it, which reads like a description of the siege. If the Gospels describe the city's fall, they were written after it.

Put at full strength, the objection says that the Gospels are not the memoirs of eyewitnesses but late products of communities, and whatever reached the writers had passed through decades of retelling by people with every reason to shape it. A historian who wouldn't trust a biography written forty years after its subject by someone who never met him shouldn't trust these.

sections.heading: What is true in it
sections.body:
The dates most scholars give are honestly arrived at, and Christians shouldn't speak as if they were a conspiracy of unbelief. Many believing scholars accept them. The temple passages are a real argument for a date around or after 70, and the reasons for the majority dates of Matthew and Luke, their use of Mark among them, are reasons a careful reader can weigh. The Study Bible's introductions to the four Gospels set them out.

It's also true that, on the church's own tradition, Mark and Luke weren't among Jesus' followers. Papias reports that Mark had not heard the Lord, and Luke says in his preface that he investigated what eyewitnesses handed down, not that he was one. Whoever wrote the Gospels wrote in Greek, mostly for readers outside Palestine. And a gap of decades is a gap. People forget, embellish and reshape. If anyone says the Gospels are as good as a transcript made on the day, he has said more than the evidence allows.

Christians have sometimes overclaimed in the other direction too. Early dates for every Gospel, before 70 or even before 50, are sometimes offered as though they were the settled result of scholarship and the later dates mere prejudice. They aren't. The early dates are a minority view, held by able scholars for real reasons, and they have to be argued, not assumed.

sections.heading: The evidence
sections.body:
Start with the dates and why they're given. Most scholars date Mark between the late 60s and the early 70s, and the debate within that range turns largely on chapter 13. Some read it as written during the Jewish revolt, when the temple was threatened but still standing, and note that it doesn't describe the city's fall in the detail one would expect after the event. Others hold that the destruction stands behind it. Matthew is usually placed between about 80 and 95 and Luke between about 75 and 90, because both seem to use Mark and because passages such as the king who burns a city in Matthew's parable of the wedding feast, and Luke's armies around Jerusalem, read to many as looking back on 70. John is usually dated to the 90s. The latest possible dates are set from outside. Ignatius of Antioch, around 110 on the usual dating, and the Didache appear to know Matthew. Marcion used a form of Luke by about 144. Papias, early in the second century, knew of writings by Mark and Matthew. And a papyrus scrap of John, P52, is usually dated to the first half of the second century, though its date is argued.

The earlier dates have serious defenders. Adolf von Harnack in 1911, John A. T. Robinson in *Redating the New Testament* (1976) and Colin Hemer in 1989 argued that Acts was written in the early 60s, because it ends with Paul under house arrest in Rome around 60 to 62 and says nothing of his death, Nero's persecution or the fall of Jerusalem; if Acts was written then, Luke, its first volume, was earlier still, and Mark before it. James Crossley, in *The Date of Mark's Gospel* (2004), argued from Mark's assumption that Jesus kept the Jewish law in full that Mark was written in the late 30s or early 40s, and that chapter 13 fits other crises, among them the emperor Caligula's attempt to set up his statue in the temple. At the other end, Richard Pervo, in *Dating Acts* (2006), placed Acts around 115. The answers to the temple argument are worth stating fairly: a burned city was a stock picture of judgment in Israel's prophets, Luke's siege language echoes their siege oracles, and a historian who allows that Jesus could foresee the temple's fall doesn't need to date the text after the event to explain it.

Now set the gap beside the evidence we have from before it. Paul's first letter to the Thessalonians is usually dated around 49 to 51, and his first letter to the Corinthians to the mid-50s. In 1 Corinthians 15 Paul hands on a summary of the faith that he says he himself received: that Christ died for our sins, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to Peter, to the Twelve, and to more than five hundred brothers at one time, "most of whom are still alive." Most scholars, including many with no stake in Christianity, think that summary took shape within a few years of the events. In Galatians Paul says that three years after his conversion he went up to Jerusalem to see Peter and stayed with him fifteen days, and that he later met James, Peter and John, whom he calls pillars. Whatever one thinks of the Gospels, the central claims they tell at length were being proclaimed in fixed form within about twenty-five years of the crucifixion, in a summary most scholars think was older still, by a man who had spent two weeks with Peter.

Finally, consider what historians of the ancient world do with gaps. One of the main surviving accounts of Alexander the Great's campaigns, Arrian's, was written more than four centuries after them. Arrian built it chiefly on the lost memoirs of two men who had served with Alexander, Ptolemy and Aristobulus, and historians use it critically, some, like A. B. Bosworth, judging it less reliable than its reputation. The comparison doesn't prove the Gospels true. It shows that the question a historian asks isn't simply how long the gap was, but what stood within it.

sections.heading: The argument, laid out
sections.intro: This is an argument about what the gap allows.
steps: On the dating most scholars hold, the Gospels were written between about thirty-five and sixty-five years after the crucifixion; a minority dates some of them sooner, and a few date Luke and Acts later.
A gap of that length falls within a single lifetime, when people who had known Jesus, and many more who had known them, were still alive.
The central claims the Gospels narrate were already being proclaimed in fixed form, within about twenty-five years, by Paul, who had met Peter, James and John.
sections.conclusion: So: the decades between Jesus and the Gospels are not an empty space in which anything could grow unchecked. They were filled by living witnesses and by an earlier written tradition that agrees on the core. That doesn't prove that every story in the Gospels is accurate. It does mean that the dates alone give no reason to doubt it.
sections.after: The weight sits on the second step. It is where Ehrman and Richard Bauckham part company, and the next section takes up the reply.

sections.heading: The strongest reply, and an answer
sections.body:
The strongest reply says that living witnesses only help if the Gospel writers used them, and there's no sign they did. A witness alive in Jerusalem in 70 is no help to a writer in Rome or Antioch who never met him. Memory, even an eyewitness's, is fragile and reconstructive, and the communities that told the stories in the meantime had their own needs. The presence of eyewitnesses somewhere in the world doesn't make a text written by someone else their testimony.

That is a fair reply, and it is the real debate. Richard Bauckham, in *Jesus and the Eyewitnesses* (2006; second edition 2017), argued that the Gospels do show signs of their sources. He pointed out that Mark names Simon of Cyrene as the father of Alexander and Rufus, as though his readers knew them, while Matthew and Luke drop the sons, and he argued that named minor figures like these were people a first audience could ask, and he compared the names in the Gospels with the names in use among Palestinian Jews of the time, as collected by Tal Ilan, and found that they fit. His critics have pressed hard, and the statistics of the names have been challenged. Samuel Byrskog's response in the *Journal for the Study of the Historical Jesus* (2008) is titled "The Eyewitnesses as Interpreters of the Past," and the title names the issue: a witness interprets what he saw as well as remembering it. Ehrman's 2016 book answers Bauckham from the psychology of memory. Bauckham himself wrote that eyewitness memory can be very unreliable and that his argument doesn't guarantee the accuracy of everything in the Gospels.

So the reply is right that eyewitnesses alive somewhere aren't enough. But it isn't the case that there's no sign the writers used them. Luke says he did. John's closing verses name a witness behind the book. Papias, early in the second century, said Mark wrote down what Peter remembered, and Paul's letters show Peter, James and John at the center of the Jerusalem church in the years he describes, not lost in some distant village. A tradition told in churches where those men had preached, and where people who had heard them were still alive, wasn't free to drift wherever a community wished. Whether it was kept well is the question of how oral tradition worked, and the next page takes it up.

sections.heading: What remains unresolved
sections.body: The dates themselves are unresolved within limits. Mark could be from the late 60s or the early 70s; a minority would place it decades earlier, a few later. Luke and Acts range from the early 60s to the second century in serious scholarship, and the end of Acts is read both as a sign of an early date and as a deliberate literary choice. Whether Bauckham's eyewitness thesis holds is argued, and some of his particular arguments, the statistics of the names among them, are contested even by scholars who share his conclusions. And no date can tell us by itself how faithfully the tradition was kept. Those questions are open, and a reader who wants certainty about them will not get it from anyone honest.

sections.heading: Where Christians differ
sections.body: Faithful Christians differ on when the Gospels were written, and this page takes no side. Many evangelical scholars date the Synoptic Gospels to the 60s or earlier; many others, evangelicals among them, accept the majority dates after 70. Christians also differ on how to read the temple prophecies, as words of Jesus preserved before the event or as words remembered and set down after it, and both views are held by people who confess that Jesus truly foretold Jerusalem's fall. What the church confesses doesn't depend on a decade. It depends on whether the Gospels tell the truth about a man who was crucified under Pontius Pilate and raised on the third day, and the earliest evidence for that claim, in Paul's letters, is earlier than any of the four.
